pop_quiz_song1.question:
What word best completes this line in the poem?
'Through galaxies of stars and _____'

options.text: A. flies
B. skies
C. moo
D. blue

A.text: Rhymes with 'eyes', but doesn't make sense in context.

B.text: Fits the rhyme and the meaning! Also surreal and poetic!

C.text: Rhymes with 'through', but too silly for the line.

D.text: Rhymes with 'through', completely offbeat. Try another choice!

pop_quiz_song2.question:
What word completes this line best?
'Deep in the ocean, where echoes _____'

options.text: A. flow
B. grow
C. mow
D. cat

A.text: A good rhyming and thematic fit!

B.text: Rhymes well, but doesn't match the imagery of sound/echoes.

C.text: Too goofy. doesn't match the tone or rhyme.

D.text: No rhyme and unrelated to the ocean theme.

pop_quiz_song3.question:
Which word fits here?
'In moonlit gardens, where shadows _____'

options.text: A. dance
B. prance
C. enhance
D. romance

A.text: Beautiful rhyme and fits the poetic tone.

B.text: Close rhyme, but a bit off in tone.

C.text: Rhymes, but sounds like a lunch order.

pop_quiz_llm1.question: An AI trained on massive amounts of text can understand what words mean and use that understanding to answer questions, just like a human.

options.text: True
False

true.text: Not quite. While AI can predict words and patterns very well, it doesn't actually understand meaning like humans do.

false.text: Correct! AI doesn't truly understand meaning - it's actually very good at recognizing patterns in text and predicting what words should come next.

pop_quiz_llm2.question: What best describes the role of training data when building an AI?

options.text: A. It helps the AI memorize exact sentences
B. It teaches the AI emotional understanding
C. It feeds the AI examples so it can learn word patterns
D. It teaches the AI to translate spoken language into sound

a.text: Not quite. AI doesn't just memorize sentences - it learns patterns from them.

b.text: No, AI doesn't actually develop emotional understanding from training data.

c.text: Correct! Training data helps the AI learn patterns in how words and phrases are used together.

d.text: No, text training data isn't about sound translation.

pop_quiz_llm3.question:
After reading these phrases:
'The sun is shining.'
'The sun rises in the east.'
'The sun sets beautifully.'

What is the AI most likely to predict after seeing: 'The sun…'

options.text: A. sleeps
B. dances
C. is
D. explodes

a.text: No, 'sleeps' wasn't in any of the training examples.

b.text: No, 'dances' wasn't in any of the training examples.

c.text: Correct! Based on the training examples, 'is' appeared after 'The sun' and is therefore most likely to be predicted.

d.text: No, 'explodes' wasn't in any of the training examples.

pop_quiz_prompt1.question: What makes a prompt more likely to give a useful response from an AI?

options.text: A. Keeping it very short
B. Being vague so the AI can be creative
C. Giving clear, specific instructions
D. Asking multiple unrelated things at once

a.text: Short prompts can be helpful, but not if they leave out important details.

b.text: Vague prompts often lead to vague answers.

c.text: Yes! Clear, specific prompts help the AI understand exactly what you're looking for.

d.text: Too many unrelated requests can confuse the AI.

pop_quiz_prompt2.question: Which of these is the best prompt for writing a travel blog post?

options.text: A. Write about travel.
B. Tell me something interesting.
C. Describe a trip.
D. Write a 3-paragraph blog post about visiting Jaipur, focusing on culture, food, and historical sites.

a.text: That's too vague and won't guide the AI well.

b.text: This prompt doesn't give enough direction or context.

c.text: It's slightly better, but still too general.

d.text: Correct! This prompt is specific and gives the AI clear instructions on content and structure.

pop_quiz_prompt3.question: What should you do if the AI's response isn't quite right the first time?

options.text: A. Give up
B. Keep repeating the same prompt
C. Refine the prompt with more detail or clarity
D. Complain to the AI

a.text: No need to give up! Try adjusting your prompt.

b.text: Repeating the same thing usually leads to the same result.

c.text: Exactly! Improving your prompt is the best way to guide the AI toward a better response.

d.text: That won't help. Instead, focus on giving clearer instructions.

pop_quiz_prompt4.question: Why is it helpful to set a “role” in your prompt, like saying 'You are a teacher…'?

options.text: A. So the AI knows how to behave or what tone to use
B. To make the prompt longer
C. It confuses the AI
D. It's required for the AI to work

a.text: Yes! Giving the AI a role helps it tailor its response to your needs.

b.text: Making the prompt longer isn't helpful unless it adds useful detail.

c.text: Actually, roles help guide the AI—they don't confuse it.

d.text: It's not required, but it definitely improves the results.

pop_quiz_model1.question: Which of the following best describes how a machine learning model differs from a traditional mathematical formula?

options.text: A) A machine learning model is always smaller and easier to interpret than a traditional formula.
B) A machine learning model is a fixed set of rules written by humans.
C) A machine learning model has billions of parameters that are learned from data, not directly written by humans.
D) A machine learning model can only process numbers, whereas traditional formulas can process words and images.

a.text: Machine learning models are often very complex and can be difficult to interpret.

b.text: Unlike traditional formulas, machine learning models learn their rules from data, rather than having them explicitly programmed.

c.text: Correct! Machine learning models, especially large ones, have a vast number of parameters that are adjusted through training on data.

d.text: Machine learning models are highly versatile and can process various types of data, including text, images, and audio.

pop_quiz_model2.question: Why can a machine learning model “inherit” biases from its training data?

options.text: A) Because the model is programmed to ignore all data except for biased examples.
B) Because the model statistically reflects the patterns and flaws present in the data it is trained on.
C) Because the model automatically corrects any errors in the data during training.
D) Because the model only uses data that has been manually selected for fairness.

a.text: Models are not programmed to ignore data; they learn from all data provided.

b.text: Correct! If the training data contains biases, the model will learn and reflect those biases in its outputs.

c.text: Models do not automatically correct errors or biases in the data; careful data preparation and model design are needed to address this.

d.text: Not all training data is manually selected for fairness, and even then, biases can still inadvertently be present.

pop_quiz_model3.question: What is the main purpose of the feedback loop during a model's training process?

options.text: A) To randomly change the model’s parameters and hope for better results.
B) To make predictions, compare them to correct answers, and adjust parameters to reduce errors over time.
C) To permanently lock the model’s parameters after the first round of training.
D) To delete any data that the model gets wrong.

a.text: While parameters are changed, it's not random; it's a calculated adjustment based on error.

b.text: Correct! The feedback loop is essential for iterative improvement, allowing the model to learn from its mistakes and refine its predictions.

c.text: The feedback loop is about continuous adjustment, not locking parameters.

d.text: The feedback loop uses errors to adjust the model, not to delete data.

pop_quiz_thinking1.question: What does an artificial neural network primarily do when processing information?

options.text: A) It thinks and understands like a human brain.
B) It performs millions of mathematical calculations to find patterns and make predictions.
C) It randomly generates answers without using any data.
D) It memorizes every example it has ever seen.

a.text: Neural networks do not think or understand; they calculate using math.

b.text: Correct! Neural networks process information by performing fast, complex calculations to spot patterns and make predictions.

c.text: AI models rely on data and patterns, not random guessing.

d.text: While models learn from examples, they generalize patterns rather than memorizing every detail.

pop_quiz_thinking2.question: How does an AI model like a language model 'learn' to generate text?

options.text: A) By reading and truly understanding every sentence.
B) By finding statistical patterns in huge amounts of text data.
C) By copying and pasting sentences from its training data.
D) By asking humans for the correct answer each time.

a.text: AI models do not understand text; they analyze patterns.

b.text: Correct! Language models learn by identifying statistical patterns in massive datasets.

c.text: AI generates new text based on patterns, not by copying directly.

d.text: AI models learn from data, not by asking humans during generation.

pop_quiz_thinking3.question: What is the main difference between how AI and humans approach problem-solving?

options.text: A) AI uses logic and math, while humans also use intuition and emotion.
B) AI is always aware of the meaning behind its answers.
C) Humans cannot make mistakes, but AI can.
D) AI feels emotions just like humans do.

a.text: Correct! AI relies on logic and math, while humans bring intuition, emotion, and ethical reasoning.

b.text: AI does not have awareness or understanding of meaning.

c.text: Both AI and humans can make mistakes, but for different reasons.

d.text: AI does not experience emotions.

pop_quiz_pattern_matching.question: Why does an AI often give generic answers when given a vague prompt?

options.text: A) Because AI tries to match the most common patterns it has seen in its training data.
B) Because AI can read your mind and knows exactly what you want.
C) Because AI refuses to answer unless the prompt is perfect.
D) Because AI is programmed to ignore vague questions.

a.text: Correct! When the prompt is vague, AI relies on the most common patterns from its training data, leading to generic responses.

b.text: AI cannot read your mind or know your intent without clear instructions.

c.text: AI will attempt to answer any prompt, but vague prompts result in less focused answers.

d.text: AI does not ignore vague questions; it just struggles to provide specific answers.

pop_quiz_prompt_engineering.question: How does giving more context and structure in your prompt affect an AI's response?

options.text: A) It helps the AI focus on relevant patterns and produce a more accurate answer.
B) It confuses the AI and makes its answer worse.
C) It has no effect; AI always gives the same answer.
D) It makes the AI ignore your instructions.

a.text: Correct! Clear, structured prompts guide the AI to search for the most relevant information and produce better answers.

b.text: More context actually helps the AI, rather than confusing it.

c.text: The quality of the answer depends on the quality of the prompt.

d.text: AI does not ignore instructions; it tries to follow them as best as it can.

pop_quiz_iteration.question: What best describes the process of improving an AI’s answers through feedback?

options.text: A) Each new prompt and feedback helps the AI adjust its response in real time.
B) The AI permanently remembers all feedback from every user.
C) Feedback has no impact; the AI always gives the same answer.
D) Feedback makes the AI stop responding.

a.text: Correct! Your feedback acts as a new prompt, guiding the AI to refine its response during the conversation.

b.text: AI does not permanently remember feedback from individual users for privacy and safety reasons.

c.text: Feedback allows you to guide and improve the AI’s answers in real time.

d.text: Feedback helps the AI, not hinders it.

pop_quiz_ai_strengths_01.question: Why are AI tools especially good at tasks like summarizing articles or generating lists of ideas?

options.text: A) Because AI can understand emotions and context perfectly.
B) Because AI is trained on huge datasets and can spot patterns quickly.
C) Because AI always knows what you want without being told.
D) Because AI can make personal decisions for you.

a.text: AI does not truly understand emotions or context; it works by recognizing patterns in data.

b.text: Correct! AI excels at these tasks because it is trained on massive datasets and can quickly find and organize patterns.

c.text: AI cannot read your mind; it needs clear instructions to be effective.

d.text: AI cannot make personal decisions; it can only suggest options based on patterns.

pop_quiz_ai_limits_01.question: What is a key reason AI struggles with giving personal advice or showing empathy?

options.text: A) AI has too many feelings to process.
B) AI only repeats patterns from its training data and lacks real understanding.
C) AI can only answer math questions.
D) AI is programmed to ignore personal questions.

a.text: AI does not have feelings at all.

b.text: Correct! AI lacks real understanding or experience, so it can only echo patterns from its training data.

c.text: AI can answer many types of questions, not just math.

d.text: AI will try to answer, but its responses lack personal insight.

pop_quiz_human_ai_team_01.question: Why do the best results often come from humans and AI working together?

options.text: A) Because AI can replace all human creativity.
B) Because humans and AI both have the exact same strengths.
C) Because humans bring judgment and creativity, while AI brings speed and structure.
D) Because AI can make emotional decisions for humans.

a.text: AI cannot replace human creativity; it can only assist.

b.text: Humans and AI have different strengths that complement each other.

c.text: Correct! The best results come when humans use their creativity and judgment, and AI adds speed and structure.

d.text: AI does not have emotions and cannot make emotional decisions.

pop_quiz_ai_draft_01.question: Why is AI-generated text often considered a 'first draft' rather than a finished product?

options.text: A) AI always writes in perfect grammar and style.
B) AI generates text by predicting likely next words, not by understanding meaning.
C) AI only copies and pastes from existing websites.
D) AI can only answer yes/no questions.

a.text: AI can make grammar errors and often needs editing for clarity and style.

b.text: Correct! AI predicts the next word based on patterns in its training data, not by truly understanding the content.

c.text: AI does not copy and paste; it generates new text based on learned patterns.

d.text: AI can generate many types of responses, not just yes/no answers.

options.text: A) When AI repeats the same answer multiple times.
B) When AI generates information that sounds plausible but is actually false or made up.
C) When AI refuses to answer a question.
D) When AI outputs text in a different language.

a.text: Repetition is not the same as hallucination.

b.text: Correct! An AI hallucination is when the model invents facts or details that sound real but aren't true.

c.text: Refusing to answer is not a hallucination.

d.text: Changing language is not related to hallucinations.

pop_quiz_ai_voice_03.question: Why does AI-generated text often sound generic or bland?

options.text: A) AI is programmed to use only technical language.
B) AI tries to average out many writing styles to be broadly acceptable.
C) AI is unable to form complete sentences.
D) AI is designed to always use humor.

a.text: AI is not limited to technical language; it can use many styles.

b.text: Correct! AI is trained on a wide range of sources and tends to produce neutral, average-sounding text to avoid mistakes or offense.

c.text: AI can form complete sentences, but they may lack personality.

d.text: AI is not specifically designed to use humor.

pop_quiz_ai_ethics_01.question: Why can an AI system trained on biased data still appear to perform 'accurately'?

options.text: A) Because biased data always leads to better generalization.
B) Because the training algorithm automatically removes bias during optimization.
C) Because it may simply learn to reproduce patterns in the data, even if they are unfair.
D) Because performance metrics can detect and reject unfair models.

a.text: Biased data often hurts generalization—it doesn't help!

b.text: Most training algorithms do not correct for bias unless explicitly told to.

c.text: Correct! AI often mirrors patterns in data, even when those patterns are biased or unfair.

d.text: Performance metrics alone can miss ethical problems unless designed to spot them.

pop_quiz_ai_ethics_02.question: Which of the following design decisions could introduce bias into an AI system?

options.text: A) Choosing to test the model on a wide variety of scenarios.
B) Only using data labeled by a small, homogenous group of people.
C) Regularly updating your dataset with new user feedback.
D) Training the system in multiple languages.

a.text: Testing on varied scenarios actually helps reduce bias!

b.text: Correct! A limited or non-diverse labeling group can unintentionally encode their own biases into the dataset.

c.text: Updating with feedback helps catch and fix bias—this is good practice.

d.text: Multilingual training can actually improve inclusivity and generalization.

pop_quiz_ai_ethics_03.question: Which statement BEST reflects the challenge of defining fairness in AI?

options.text: A) Fairness means treating everyone exactly the same, always.
B) Fairness is built into AI systems automatically during training.
C) Fairness can mean different things depending on the context and goals of the system.
D) Fairness is purely a technical problem with a clear mathematical solution.

a.text: Treating everyone the same sounds good, but it can ignore deeper inequities.

b.text: Fairness isn’t automatic; it must be intentionally designed and tested for.

c.text: Correct! Definitions of fairness vary across use cases, cultures, and ethical frameworks.

d.text: While math can help, fairness also includes moral and social considerations.

pop_quiz_ai_responsibility_01.question: Why can't an AI system be held legally responsible when something goes wrong?

options.text: A) Because AI systems often ignore rules on purpose.
B) Because responsibility for actions always belongs to the human designers, users, or companies behind the system.
C) Because AI systems can't process information.
D) Because AI systems are registered legal entities.

a.text: AI systems don't have intentions and can't choose to ignore rules.

b.text: Correct! AI doesn't have moral or legal agency—humans and organizations are responsible for its actions.

c.text: AI systems do process information, but lack awareness or intent.

d.text: AI systems are not legal persons or entities that can be sued or fined.

pop_quiz_ai_responsibility_02.question: In a scenario where a self-driving car makes a harmful mistake, what makes assigning responsibility so complicated?

options.text: A) Only the car company should ever be liable.
B) Because multiple parties—like engineers, the company, regulators, and users—may have all played a role.
C) Responsibility is never shared between people in AI projects.
D) Self-driving cars are fully autonomous and need no human oversight.

a.text: Often, more than one group shares responsibility.

b.text: Correct! Each group can influence the outcome, from design to rules to actual use.

c.text: In reality, responsibility is often spread across many people and organizations.

d.text: Even the best AI systems need human and legal oversight.

pop_quiz_ai_responsibility_03.question: Which best describes how safer AI systems are typically built?

options.text: A) By letting the AI learn from its mistakes completely unsupervised.
B) By having only one team check all the code right before launch.
C) Through shared responsibility: engineers, companies, regulators, and users all play a role in making and using the system safely.
D) By never updating the AI once it is deployed.

a.text: Unsupervised learning without checks can lead to risky or biased behavior.

b.text: Wider review and broad accountability are needed, not just a last-minute check.

c.text: Correct! Safe AI comes from a system where everyone—builders, companies, government, and users—share responsibility.

d.text: AI should be monitored, updated, and improved over time.

pop_quiz_ai_explainability_01.question: What is meant by calling an AI system a 'black box'?

options.text: A) The AI uses physical boxes to store data.
B) We know exactly how an AI's decisions are made, step-by-step.
C) The process inside the AI is too complex or hidden for humans to easily understand.
D) The AI system always gives random outputs.

a.text: A 'black box' is not about physical boxes—it’s about a lack of interpretability.

b.text: If we understood every step, it wouldn’t be a black box.

c.text: Correct! A system is a 'black box' when we can't fully explain or follow how it reaches a decision.

d.text: Black box AI can be very consistent; the issue is the lack of transparency, not randomness.

pop_quiz_ai_explainability_02.question: Why is explainability especially important for AI decisions in fields like medicine or finance?

options.text: A) Because these fields only use simple algorithms.
B) Because lives and major opportunities can be affected, and people need to understand or challenge decisions.
C) Because everyone already understands how AI works.
D) Because AI is always more accurate without explanations.

a.text: Complex, high-stakes decisions are common in these fields, not simple algorithms.

b.text: Correct! High-stakes decisions require transparency so people can trust, audit, or contest them.

c.text: In fact, most people do NOT fully understand how AI works inside.

d.text: Lack of explanation may lead to mistrust, not better accuracy.

pop_quiz_ai_explainability_03.question: Which is a common method for making AI decisions more explainable?

options.text: A) Ignoring the inputs used by the AI.
B) Developing tools that highlight which features (like pixels, words, or numbers) were most important for a decision.
C) Making the AI guess randomly.
D) Letting only computers interpret other computers’ outputs.

a.text: Ignoring input removes useful information and makes models less transparent.

b.text: Correct! Feature highlighting, like saliency maps or feature importance scores, helps make decisions understandable.

c.text: Random guessing would reduce trust and usefulness, not increase explainability.

d.text: Explainability matters most when humans can interpret and act on AI explanations.

pop_quiz_ai_dataquality_01.question: Why can bias in training data lead to unfair AI decisions?

options.text: A) Because AI can detect and fix bias automatically.
B) Because AI will often reflect and even amplify any patterns—including bias—it finds in its training data.
C) Because biased data always makes AI less accurate, but not unfair.
D) Because AI ignores the training data after deployment.

a.text: Most AI systems don’t automatically recognize or remove bias—this requires special analysis and engineering.

b.text: Correct! AI internalizes statistical patterns, so if bias is present in the training set, it will likely appear in the results as well or even become worse.

c.text: Biased data can make AI both inaccurate and unfair, especially if the bias is systematic.

d.text: AI relies on its training data long after deployment to make new decisions.

pop_quiz_ai_dataquality_02.question: What does 'Garbage In, Garbage Out' mean when it comes to AI?

options.text: A) As long as the algorithm is complex, input data quality does not matter.
B) Good algorithms can always overcome bad data.
C) If the input data is flawed or biased, the AI's output will also be flawed or biased.
D) AI can guess the right answer without any good data.

a.text: Even the most advanced algorithms cannot make good decisions from poor data.

b.text: No AI can 'fix' bad data without specific tools or steps for quality control.

c.text: Correct! Low-quality inputs produce low-quality outputs, no matter how good the model is.

d.text: AI needs accurate, high-quality data to make good predictions or decisions.

pop_quiz_ai_dataquality_03.question: Which approach helps ensure AI systems are less likely to produce biased results?

options.text: A) Training only on historic data without review.
B) Regularly analyzing and updating datasets for fairness and representation.
C) Ignoring the data source and focusing only on the model architecture.
D) Using as little data as possible so the model stays simple.

a.text: Historic data often contains hidden biases; without review, these can be reinforced.

b.text: Correct! Routinely checking and diversifying data helps catch and reduce bias before it enters the model.

c.text: The data source is crucial—model design and data quality must both be addressed.

d.text: Less data is not better if it isn’t representative or diverse.

pop_quiz_using_ai_tools_01.question: When you use AI to generate writing, what is the safest way to avoid plagiarism?

options.text: A) Submit the AI output unchanged, since AI creates original text.
B) Rewrite the text in your own style, add your own insights, and note where AI helped.
C) Only change a few words so it looks different.
D) Avoid using AI for any writing tasks.

a.text: Submitting raw AI text can still be plagiarism if it doesn't reflect your thinking.

b.text: Correct! Personalizing, adding insights, and giving credit are the best ways to avoid plagiarism.

c.text: Simple word swaps can leave the structure and ideas unchanged, which is not enough.

d.text: You can use AI if you do so responsibly and transparently.

pop_quiz_using_ai_tools_02.question: Why does AI sometimes include information that is outdated, inaccurate, or even made up ('hallucination')?

options.text: A) AI always searches the current internet for answers.
B) AI can't access any information at all.
C) AI generates responses based on statistical patterns from its training data, not real-time knowledge.
D) AI purposefully tries to confuse users.

a.text: AI models do not browse the web for current info when generating text.

b.text: AI uses what it has 'learned' in training, not nothing.

c.text: Correct! AI predicts the next word based on data it has seen during training, which can lead to errors or made-up info.

d.text: AI is not trying to confuse you; it has no intentions, only algorithms.

pop_quiz_using_ai_tools_03.question: Which statement best explains why a 'transparency note' matters when using AI for writing assignments?

options.text: A) It helps teachers understand what was AI-generated and what was your own thinking.
B) It adds more words to your essay for a higher word count.
C) It is required by law in all schools.
D) It hides any use of AI so you get more credit.

a.text: Correct! Transparency notes increase trust and clarify your process to teachers or reviewers.

b.text: The purpose is honesty, not padding length.

c.text: It's not a universal law, but it's an important practice.

d.text: Transparency means being open, not hiding your AI use.

pop_quiz_ai_deepfake_01.question: Which technique is most commonly used to create hyper-realistic deepfakes?

options.text: A) Decision Trees
B) Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs)
C) K-Means Clustering
D) Nearest Neighbor Algorithms

a.text: Decision Trees are useful for classification tasks, not for generating realistic images.

b.text: Correct! GANs are commonly used to create convincing deepfakes by training one AI to generate images and another to detect fakes.

c.text: K-Means Clustering is used for grouping similar data, not for generating images.

d.text: Nearest Neighbor algorithms are used for matching, not for image synthesis.

pop_quiz_ai_deepfake_02.question: Why can AI-generated misinformation spread faster than traditional rumors?

options.text: A) AI can make sure every message is true before sharing it.
B) AI models understand the difference between truth and lies.
C) AI can generate large quantities of convincing content very quickly.
D) AI requires human approval for every post it generates.

a.text: AI can't verify the truth of its outputs; it generates content based on patterns.

b.text: AI does not inherently know what is true or false.

c.text: Correct! AI allows for the rapid, large-scale creation of realistic content, helping misinformation spread much faster than before.

d.text: AI-generated content can often be posted automatically, without human checks.

pop_quiz_ai_deepfake_03.question: What is one major challenge when trying to detect AI-generated fake content?

options.text: A) Only humans can generate fake content.
B) AI fakes never look realistic.
C) Detection tools rely on clues that AI models are constantly improving at hiding.
D) AI-generated content always carries a digital watermark.

a.text: AI is very capable of generating fake content—sometimes more persuasively than humans.

b.text: Modern AI-generated fakes can look extremely real, which is a big part of the problem.

c.text: Correct! As AI-generated content gets better at hiding its tracks, detection tools must constantly keep improving to catch new tricks.

d.text: Not all AI-generated content is watermarked or easy to trace.
